title: Kidilum Brings Kerala Coastal Cuisine to New York's Flatiron District
excerpt: A 74-seat restaurant helmed by Kerala-born chef Vinu Raveendran is reshaping what South Indian dining looks like in Manhattan, with a spice-grinding room, an open kitchen, and dishes rooted in the Malabar Coast.
body:
A Chef's Kerala Dream, Realized in Manhattan

On February 27, a new entrant joined Manhattan's increasingly competitive South Indian dining scene. Kidilum — slang for "beyond awesome" in Malayalam — opened its doors at 31 West 21st Street in the Flatiron District, marking the American debut of chef Vinu Raveendran and adding Kerala's coastal cuisine to a neighborhood already rich with dining options.

The 74-seat restaurant is a project of Hungry Trio Hospitality, the group led by Sammeer Raajpal and the mother-son duo Archana and Sidharth Sharma. Their portfolio spans Aarzu Indian Bistro, Ramen Nagomi, and Esquina No. 525, but Kidilum represents their most ambitious venture yet.

"When I crave Indian food, I always crave South Indian food because it's where I'm from. This is my dream come true."

— Vinu Raveendran, Chef and Partner, Kidilum

Raveendran's résumé reads like a global fine-dining itinerary. The Kerala native trained at the two-Michelin-starred Mugaritz in San Sebastián, Spain, before serving as executive chef at Carnival by Trèsind in Dubai. He left Dubai for New York in 2024, pitching his concept to Hungry Trio's founders, and spent the next two years developing Kidilum's menu and identity.

Malabar Coast on the Menu

The menu draws from Kerala's coastal traditions, with particular emphasis on the tea shop culture Raveendran grew up with during summer vacations at his cousin's shop. Every meal begins with a complimentary amuse bouche: a mini steamed idli dusted with podi (a roasted lentil and spice powder) served tableside with whipped coconut chutney.

Signature dishes include a nandu crab curry with roasted coconut, thalasherry biriyani with goat, vella lamb korma (a white lamb shank preparation with burnt garlic oil), and pollichathu — prawns roasted in banana leaves with onion tomato marmalade. An Alleppey fish curry made with barramundi and raw mango, and a pork vindaloo that nods to Kerala's Portuguese colonial history, round out the mains.

Raveendran has also introduced a paper podi dosa, joining the ranks of those found at fellow South Indian restaurants Semma and Kanyakumari. Desserts include pradhaman made with lentils, jaggery, salted cashews, and lemon pickle jam, alongside a Calicut halwa served with Malabar vanilla ice cream and praline.

Part of a Broader South Indian Wave

Kidilum arrives at a moment when South Indian cuisine is carving out significant real estate in New York's dining landscape. Semma, which opened in Greenwich Village in 2022, earned a Michelin star. Kanyakumari brought coastal Southern Indian food to Union Square in 2024 and joined the Michelin Guide that June. Chatti by Regi Mathew introduced Kerala's toddy shop culture to Midtown, while Lungi added to the genre's growing presence.

For members of the Indian diaspora who grew up with these flavors, the shift represents a long-overdue correction. For decades, Northern Indian cuisine — butter chicken, naan, tikka masala — dominated the city's perception of Indian food. The new wave of hyper-regional restaurants is introducing New Yorkers to the diversity that exists within the subcontinent's culinary traditions.

"Hyper-regional cuisine is not a risk in New York, it's a strength," Raveendran told Marketspoon. "We're not trying to simplify Kerala to make it easier. We're inviting people to discover it."

What's Next

With a 4.8 rating on Resy across more than 900 reviews and a ranking as Beli's No. 2 Best New NYC Restaurant, Kidilum has quickly established itself as one of the city's hardest-to-get reservations. Tables are released daily at 11 a.m. EST, two weeks in advance, and book almost instantly. Walk-ins are accommodated at the bar, which seats eight with four additional high-top tables.

Co-founder Sidharth Sharma has noted that the Flatiron location was deliberate. "We chose Flatiron because we instantly fell in love with its energy," he said. "The kind of neighborhood where creativity, culture, and dining are always evolving."

The 74-seat space, designed with carved-wood screens, brass fixtures, and earth-toned banquettes inspired by traditional Nalukettu courtyard homes, is open Tuesday through Sunday from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. Reservations are available via Resy.
